questions.question: Why does Python use indentation (spaces) instead of curly braces `{ }`?
options: It doesn't — Python uses curly braces just like most languages
Indentation defines which lines of code belong inside a loop, conditional, or function, and incorrect indentation is a real syntax error
Indentation is optional and purely stylistic
Python only runs code written on a single line
questions.explanation: Python uses indentation, not braces, to group code blocks. This makes code visually consistent but also means indentation mistakes can break a script.

questions.question: What does Python's `None` typically represent?
options: The absence of a value — similar to 'null' in other languages
questions.explanation: `None` represents 'no value.' A large share of real bugs come from code expecting a real value but receiving `None` instead.

questions.question: An engineer says a script 'crashed on an unhandled exception' when calling an AI model API. Which question best identifies whether this is a production risk?
options: Why is the script written in Python instead of a faster language?
Is there a try/except around this API call, and if not, could one provider outage or bad response crash the whole service?
Can we just delete the script?
What color is the terminal text?
questions.explanation: Missing try/except error handling around external API calls means a single failure (timeout, bad response, provider outage) can crash the entire process instead of being handled gracefully.
